title: What Does Probate Cost in Washington State?
shortAnswer: Washington State (WA) law sets no fixed price for probate. Attorney fees and pay for the personal representative (executor) are not set by a percentage or fee schedule. Unless a will sets the executor's pay, the law says both must be "just and reasonable," and heirs can ask the court to review fees. Court fees are fixed by statute: in King County, opening a probate costs $290 (fee schedule effective October 1, 2026). Bond, newspaper notice, certified copies and appraisals can add to the total. Most costs are paid from the estate, not from the executor's own pocket.

sections.heading: Attorney fees: hourly, percentage, or something else?
sections.body:
Washington's probate statutes do not set attorney fees as a percentage of the estate, and they do not list hourly rates. What the law says is:

- Attorney fees for work on the estate are part of the compensation the court may allow, in an amount "the court shall deem just and reasonable" (RCW 11.48.210).
- The executor may receive extra pay if they also act as the estate's attorney.

Whether a lawyer bills hourly, by flat fee or another way is agreed between the executor and the lawyer. The law sets no typical dollar range, so none is given here.

sections.heading: How heirs can question fees
sections.body:
- **Closing with a court decree.** If an executor with "nonintervention powers" (authority to act without court approval for each step) asks the court to close the estate, the petition must "state the fees paid or proposed to be paid" to the executor, attorneys, accountants and appraisers. Any heir whose share would be reduced by those fees receives a copy. If asked, the court will "determine the reasonableness of said fees" at the hearing (RCW 11.68.100).
- **Closing with a declaration of completion.** If the executor closes the estate by filing a declaration of completion, it must list the fees paid or to be paid. A party has 30 days after it is filed to ask the court to review them. If no one does, the fees "will be deemed reasonable and will be approved" (RCW 11.68.110). Missing that deadline can end the chance to object.
- **Misconduct.** If an executor breached their duties, a party can petition the court. The court can order remedies that include money damages, removal, and attorney fees (RCW 11.68.070). If the court finds the executor did not do the job properly, it may "deny him or her any compensation whatsoever" or reduce it (RCW 11.48.210).

sections.heading: Court filing fees and copies
sections.body:
The basic probate filing fee is set by state law. RCW 36.18.020 sets a $200 fee for the person who opens a probate, plus surcharges listed in the same section. King County's clerk lists the total as:

| Item (King County Superior Court Clerk) | Fee |
|---|---|
| Probate filing | $290.00 |
| Letters of administration or testamentary | $5.00 |
| Certified copy, first page | $5.00 |
| Certified copy, each additional page | $1.00 |

*Source: King County fee schedule effective October 1, 2026, read October 11, 2026.* In other counties, check the clerk's current fee schedule.

sections.heading: Probate bond: is it required?
sections.body:
A bond protects the estate if the executor mishandles money. Under RCW 11.28.185, whether one is needed depends on the facts:

- **No bond is required** when the will shows the person did not want the executor to post one.
- **No bond is required** when the executor is the surviving spouse or domestic partner and the court finds the whole estate, after expenses and creditor claims, will go to them.
- **No bond is required** when a bank or trust company serves as executor.
- **A bond is always required** when the court appoints an outside "suitable person" because no one entitled to serve asked to within 90 days of the death (RCW 11.28.120(3)), unless that person is a bank, trust company or qualifying law firm. The bond must be "commensurate with the major probate assets." This rule took effect June 11, 2026.
- **In all other cases**, a bond is required "unless waived by the court." The court sets the amount.
- The court can require a larger bond at any time, or reduce one "upon a proper showing."

**Executors who live out of state.** A nonresident must appoint a Washington agent and "must file a bond to be approved by the court," unless bond was waived under RCW 11.28.185 (RCW 11.36.010).

The cost of a bond premium is set by the bonding company, not by law.

sections.heading: Who pays: the estate or the executor?
sections.body:
In most cases the estate pays. The executor "shall be allowed all necessary expenses in the care, management, and settlement of the estate" (RCW 11.48.050). When the estate's debts are paid, "Expenses of administration" come first, ahead of funeral costs, last-illness costs and other claims (RCW 11.76.110).

Disputes are different. In a court dispute over an estate, the judge may order costs, "including reasonable attorneys' fees," paid by any party or by the estate, and can consider "whether the litigation benefits the estate" (RCW 11.96A.150). An executor or heir may be ordered to pay costs personally.

sections.heading: Is the executor paid, and is it taxable?
sections.body:
**Pay.** Executors can be paid. If the will sets the pay, that amount is the full payment unless the executor files a written refusal with the court before qualifying as executor. If the will says nothing, or there is no will, the court sets pay that is "just and reasonable" (RCW 11.48.210). Some family executors decline payment.

**Taxes.** The IRS says: "All personal representatives must include fees paid to them from an estate in their gross income." An executor who is not in the business of serving as executor reports the fees as other income, not self-employment income (IRS Publication 559, 2025 edition). A tax professional can advise on a particular situation.

sections.heading: Other common costs
sections.body:
- **Notice to creditors.** If the executor gives notice to creditors, it must be published "once each week for three successive weeks in a legal newspaper" in the county where the estate is being handled. If the person lived in Washington but probate was opened in a different county, it is published in the county where they lived instead (RCW 11.40.020). The newspaper sets the price.
- **Appraisals and accountants.** Within three months of appointment, the executor must prepare a sworn inventory with each item's "fair net value, as of the date of the decedent's death" (RCW 11.44.015). The statute does not require a professional appraiser. Appraiser and accountant fees are among the fees disclosed at closing (RCW 11.68.100).

faqs.question: How much does a probate attorney cost in Washington?
faqs.answer: No state law sets a price or a percentage. Probate attorney fees must be "just and reasonable," and the court can review them (RCW 11.48.210). The lawyer and executor agree on billing. Before hiring, ask for the billing method and an estimate in writing.

title: Who Pays a Parent's Debts After They Die in Washington State?
shortAnswer: The estate pays, not the family. In Washington State (WA), the personal representative pays the estate's debts in an order the law sets: administration costs first, then reasonable funeral costs, then last-illness costs, and so on. Creditors usually have four months after the first published notice to file a claim, or up to 24 months after death if no notice is given. If debts exceed assets, lower-priority creditors may go unpaid. Children are generally not personally responsible, with exceptions such as co-signers and joint account holders.

sections.heading: The estate pays, not the children
sections.body:
A parent's debts become claims against the estate. The personal representative (executor) pays valid debts from estate money before anything goes to heirs.

The Federal Trade Commission says, "By law, family members do not usually have to pay the debts of a deceased relative from their own money." The exceptions: you may owe the debt yourself if you:

- **Co-signed** the loan.
- **Held a joint account,** such as a joint credit card. Being only an "authorized user" is different (CFPB).
- **Are the surviving spouse** in a community property state, or in a state that makes a spouse pay certain debts, "like some healthcare expenses" (FTC). Washington is a community property state. In a Washington estate, a community debt "is charged against the entire community property," including the surviving spouse's half (RCW 11.10.030). Washington law also makes "the expenses of the family" chargeable on the property of both spouses (RCW 26.16.205). Whether a particular debt is a community debt or a family expense depends on the facts.
- **Are the executor and did not follow** the state's probate rules (FTC).

Some property that passes outside the will can still be reached. Under RCW 11.18.200, unless a statute exempts it, a person who receives a nonprobate asset that was available to pay the parent's general debts just before death "takes the asset subject to liabilities, claims, estate taxes, and the fair share of expenses of administration." Payable-on-death accounts and houses passing by transfer on death deed are covered, "to the extent of the decedent's beneficial ownership interest in the property immediately before death." The recipient may have to account to the personal representative, who must first give notice under chapter 11.96A RCW. Life insurance paid to a named beneficiary other than the parent is protected "against the creditors and representatives of the insured" (RCW 48.18.410), but premiums paid "with intent to defraud creditors" can be recovered.

sections.heading: In what order are debts paid?
sections.body:
RCW 11.76.110 says "the reasonable expenses of administration and the enforceable debts of the estate shall be paid in the following order":

1. Expenses of administration.
2. Funeral expenses, in an amount the court orders or a personal representative with nonintervention powers finds reasonable.
3. Expenses of the last sickness, on the same reasonableness standard.
4. Wages due for work performed within 60 days before death.
5. Exemptions and awards under chapter 11.54 RCW (awards a court may make to a surviving spouse, registered domestic partner, or dependent children).
6. All other enforceable demands against the estate.

The list is "subject to federal preemption" and to the priority of liens under other law. A mortgage or other lien has priority only against the proceeds of the property it is attached to (RCW 11.76.120). Credit cards, personal loans, and most medical bills generally fall in the last class. Medical bills from the final illness are in the third class.

sections.heading: How long do creditors have to file a claim?
sections.body:
Notice to creditors is optional. A personal representative "may give notice to the creditors of the decedent" (RCW 11.40.020). If they do, the notice is published "once each week for three successive weeks" in a legal newspaper. A copy, with the parent's Social Security number, must be mailed to the DSHS Office of Financial Recovery.

RCW 11.40.051 then sets the deadlines:

- **Creditors who got actual notice:** the later of "thirty days after the personal representative's service or mailing of notice to the creditor" or "four months after the date of first publication of the notice."
- **Creditors who did not get actual notice:** four months after first publication if the creditor "was not reasonably ascertainable." If the creditor was reasonably ascertainable, they have up to 24 months after the death.
- **No notice at all:** claims must be presented "within twenty-four months after the decedent's date of death."

A late creditor "is forever barred," as to "both the decedent's probate and nonprobate assets." A claim must be signed, served on or mailed to the personal representative or their attorney, and filed with the probate court (RCW 11.40.070).

sections.heading: What if there are more debts than assets?
sections.body:
An estate whose debts exceed its assets is insolvent. Because RCW 11.76.110 requires payment "in the following order," higher classes are paid first. When money runs out, lower classes, usually credit cards and other unsecured debts, may get part of what they are owed or nothing. If there is not enough to pay one class in full, "each creditor shall be paid in proportion to his or her claim," and no lower class is paid until that class is paid in full (RCW 11.76.150).

The unpaid balance does not pass to the children (FTC, CFPB). But a child who received a nonprobate asset, such as a payable-on-death account, may have to contribute it toward the debts (RCW 11.18.200). Also:

- **Less independence for the executor.** A court grants nonintervention powers (acting without court approval at each step) only if it "determines that the decedent's estate is solvent, taking into account probate and nonprobate assets" (RCW 11.68.011). A will can also tell the court not to grant them.
- **Heirs may receive nothing.** Debts come before inheritances. When gifts must be cut back, RCW 11.10.010 sets the order: property passing without a will, then the residue, then general gifts, then specific gifts.

sections.heading: Credit cards and debt collectors
sections.body:
Credit card balances are paid from the estate as ordinary claims. A joint account holder may owe the balance personally. An authorized user generally does not (CFPB).

Collectors may discuss the debt with the executor or administrator, the spouse, and a few others. They may contact other relatives only to locate the executor (FTC, CFPB). The CFPB says collectors "are not allowed to say or hint that you are responsible for paying the debts with your own money."

sections.heading: Federal student loans
sections.body: U.S. Department of Education rules "provide for discharge of a borrower's obligation to repay those loans if the borrower dies." A Parent PLUS loan is also discharged "if the student on whose behalf the parent borrowed dies." The servicer needs proof of death, such as "an original or certified copy of the death certificate" or an accurate copy of one, or the Department may verify the death through an approved federal or state database (34 CFR 685.212(a)). These rules do not cover private student loans.

sections.heading: The house, the mortgage, and Medicaid
sections.body:
**The mortgage.** A mortgage stays attached to the house. See [What Happens to the Mortgage When a Parent Dies?](/guides/mortgage-after-death-washington)

**Medicaid estate recovery.** If a parent received Medicaid long-term care at 55 or older, Washington must seek repayment from the estate, including nonprobate assets such as a transfer on death house. Hardship waivers exist (RCW 43.20B.080). See [Medicaid and the Family Home](/long-term-care/medicaid-and-the-family-home).

title: Can a Will Be Challenged in Washington State?
shortAnswer: Yes, but the window is short. A person with an interest in a will has four months after the court admits the will to probate (or rejects it) to file a challenge. They must personally serve the personal representative within 90 days of filing. The court decides issues such as mental capacity, undue influence, fraud, and whether the will was properly signed and witnessed. If no one files and serves in time, the court's decision on the will becomes final.

sections.heading: Who can challenge a will, and how long they have
sections.body:
Washington's will contest law, chapter 11.24 RCW, lets "any person interested in any will" file a challenge. The petition must be filed "within four months immediately following the probate or rejection" of the will (RCW 11.24.010).

- **Filing starts the case.** For the deadline, a contest starts when the petition is filed, not when it is served.
- **Service within 90 days.** The challenger must personally serve the personal representative (executor) within 90 days after filing. If that does not happen, the contest is treated as never started for purposes of the four-month deadline.

If no one files and serves in time, the probate or rejection is "binding and final."

The clock runs from the court's order, not from the funeral. The court can admit a will right away (RCW 11.20.020). The personal representative must notify heirs and beneficiaries within 20 days after appointment (RCW 11.28.237).

sections.heading: On what grounds?
sections.body:
RCW 11.24.010 lists the issues the court decides:

- **Capacity.** Whether the person was competent to make a will. A will-maker must be "of sound mind" and at least 18 (RCW 11.12.010).
- **Restraint or undue influence.**
- **Fraud.** Whether the will rested on "fraudulent representations."
- **Any other cause affecting validity,** including improper signing.

A Washington will must be in writing, signed by the person (or by someone at their direction and in their presence), and witnessed by two or more competent witnesses. A will validly signed under another state's law where it was made or where the person lived also counts (RCW 11.12.020).

The order admitting the will counts as initial evidence that it is valid, and the challenger must prove otherwise (RCW 11.24.030). If all or part of the will is found invalid, that part is revoked (RCW 11.24.040).

sections.heading: What if a family member was left out?
sections.body:
Being left out is not, by itself, a listed ground. Washington law does protect two groups:

- **A child born or adopted after the will was signed** and not named or provided for. That child generally receives what they would have inherited with no will, unless the will or "clear and convincing evidence" shows the omission was intentional (RCW 11.12.091). On the same standard of proof, a court may award less if that better fits the parent's intent.
- **A spouse or domestic partner married after the will was signed.** The same basic rule applies (RCW 11.12.095). The court may consider the spouse's community property rights and anything provided outside the will.

Separately, a surviving spouse or domestic partner keeps one-half of the community property; only the other half can be left by will (RCW 11.02.070). Which assets are community property depends on the facts.

sections.heading: What if there is more than one will?
sections.body: A later will revokes an earlier one expressly or by inconsistency. So does burning, tearing, or destroying a will with intent to revoke, but only if the will-maker does it, or someone else does it in the will-maker's presence and at their direction (RCW 11.12.040). A family member who destroys a will after the death does not revoke it. If a later will that fully replaced an earlier one is itself revoked, the earlier will does not come back unless the person intended it to (RCW 11.12.080).

sections.heading: What if a beneficiary died first, or is a minor?
sections.body:
**Died first.** The anti-lapse rule (RCW 11.12.110) covers beneficiaries who descend from the will-maker's grandparent, such as children, siblings, nieces and nephews. If that beneficiary dies first and leaves descendants who outlive the will-maker, those descendants take the gift. The will can provide otherwise. Friends and in-laws are not covered. A gift that is not saved this way generally goes to the rest of the estate under the will, or under state law if the will does not say who gets the rest (RCW 11.12.120).

**A minor beneficiary.** Washington provides several routes:

- **A custodian under the Uniform Transfers to Minors Act.** The executor may transfer the gift to a custodian if the will authorizes it (RCW 11.114.050). If the will does not authorize it, the executor may still make the transfer when it is in the child's best interest and the will does not prohibit it, with court approval above $30,000 (RCW 11.114.060). The custodian generally turns the property over at 21 for will-authorized transfers and at 18 otherwise. When naming the custodian, the person making the transfer can extend this to 25, unless the will specifically says otherwise (RCW 11.114.200).
- **Up to $15,000 in 12 months** may go to the person who cares for the child and lives with them, a guardian, a custodian, or an interest-bearing account solely in the child's name. This option is not available if the person paying knows a conservator has been appointed or a conservatorship case is pending (RCW 11.130.575).
- **A conservator** appointed by the court to manage a minor's property (RCW 11.130.360).

sections.heading: Who pays the legal costs, and can it be settled?
sections.body:
If a will is overturned, costs are up to the court. If the will is upheld, the court may charge the challenger the costs. It may also charge the challenger reasonable attorney's fees, unless the challenger acted "with probable cause and in good faith" (RCW 11.24.050). Separately, under RCW 11.96A.150, the court may order fees paid by any party, by the estate, or from a nonprobate asset, and that power is not limited by RCW 11.24.050. The law sets no fee schedule.

The Trust and Estate Dispute Resolution Act (TEDRA, chapter 11.96A RCW) offers ways to settle outside court. Everyone involved can sign a binding written agreement (RCW 11.96A.220), or any party can start mediation by written notice, with the mediator's fees split equally (RCW 11.96A.300). Do not count on talks or mediation to pause the four-month deadline. The statute stops the clock only when a petition is filed (RCW 11.24.010).

For disputes about selling the family house rather than the will itself, see [What Happens If Heirs Disagree About Selling?](/guides/heirs-disagree-selling-house).

faqs.answer: Four months from the date the court admits the will to probate or rejects it. The petition must be filed within that time, and the personal representative must be personally served within 90 days after filing. Miss either step and the court's decision on the will becomes binding and final (RCW 11.24.010).

faqs.question: My brother was in Mom's will but died before she did. Is his share gone?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Washington's anti-lapse rule covers a brother, because he descends from Mom's grandparents. If he left children or other descendants who outlived Mom, they take his share, unless the will says otherwise (RCW 11.12.110). If he left no such descendants, the rest of the will or state law decides where the gift goes (RCW 11.12.120).

faqs.question: What happens if a grandchild under 18 inherits money?
faqs.answer: The executor may transfer it to a custodian under the Uniform Transfers to Minors Act. Court approval is needed over $30,000 if the will does not authorize the transfer. The custodian turns it over at 18 or 21 depending on the type of transfer, or as late as 25 if the custodianship was extended (RCW 11.114.050, .060, .200). If no conservator has been appointed, up to $15,000 in a 12-month period can go to the adult the child lives with, among other options (RCW 11.130.575).

faqs.question: Who pays the lawyers if someone contests a will?
faqs.answer: The court decides. If the will is upheld, the challenger may be charged costs. They may also be charged reasonable attorney's fees, unless they acted with probable cause and in good faith (RCW 11.24.050). The court can also order fees paid by a party, by the estate, or from a nonprobate asset (RCW 11.96A.150).

faqs.question: Can we settle without going to court?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. Under TEDRA, everyone involved can sign a written agreement that binds all interested persons (RCW 11.96A.220). Any party can also start mediation by serving written notice on the others (RCW 11.96A.300). Neither option pauses the four-month deadline; only filing a petition does (RCW 11.24.010). *General information, not legal advice. Real Property Planning does not refer anyone to attorneys.*

title: Family Member or Trust Company? Choosing a Trustee in Washington State
shortAnswer: Your trustee or successor trustee can be a family member, a friend, a professional, a bank or trust company, or co-trustees. Whoever serves owes the same duties: loyalty, impartiality, prudent investing, information and yearly statements. The law allows "reasonable compensation" but sets no fee. The real question is who can carry those duties for as long as the trust lasts, and at what cost.

sections.heading: What any trustee must do
sections.body:
The trust's terms generally control over the default rules, but no trust can excuse a trustee from acting in good faith (RCW 11.97.010). Every trustee owes these duties:

- **Loyalty.** A trustee "must administer the trust solely in the interests of the beneficiaries" (RCW 11.98.078).
- **Impartiality.** With two or more beneficiaries, the trustee must act impartially, "giving due regard to the beneficiaries' respective interests" (RCW 11.98.078).
- **Prudent investing.** The trustee must invest "as a prudent investor would" and diversify unless special circumstances make that unwise or the trust says otherwise. A trustee with special skills, or named because they claimed them, must use them (RCW 11.100.020, 11.100.047).
- **Information.** The trustee must keep qualified beneficiaries "reasonably informed." For a trust that became irrevocable after December 31, 2011, the trustee must also notify them within 60 days of accepting the role, unless the trustor waived or changed that requirement. A narrow exception applies when the trustor's spouse or domestic partner has capacity, is the only current beneficiary, and everyone else is a descendant of the couple (RCW 11.98.072).
- **Yearly statements.** At least once a year, the trustee must send each beneficiary currently eligible for distributions an itemized statement of receipts and disbursements. An adult beneficiary can waive it in writing (RCW 11.106.020, 11.106.100).

While you are alive and the trust is revocable, only you are entitled to that information (RCW 11.98.072). See [For Trustees](/trustees) for the trustee's side.

sections.heading: Who can serve
sections.body:
**Individuals.** Chapter 11.98 RCW has no section setting qualifications for an individual trustee. The disqualification list in RCW 11.36.010 (minors, people of unsound mind, felons) covers probate personal representatives, not trustees. Individuals do not need a state certificate to act (RCW 30B.04.040).

**Banks and trust companies.** A company doing trust business here generally must be authorized, such as a state trust company certified by the Department of Financial Institutions (DFI), a state bank with trust powers, a national bank authorized by the Comptroller of the Currency, or an out-of-state trust institution approved by DFI (RCW 30B.04.030, 30B.04.050). DFI publishes a list of the trust companies it regulates.

**Out of state.** An out-of-state trust institution that meets Washington's requirements need not keep a Washington office (RCW 30B.38.005). Naming an out-of-state trustee "does not change the situs of the trust" (RCW 11.98.039).

sections.heading: What a trustee can be paid
sections.body: A trustee may receive "reasonable compensation," based on "the time, effort, skill, and responsibility involved" (RCW 11.98.070(26)). The statute sets no percentage. The trust document can set, limit or waive pay (RCW 11.97.010). Institutions set their own fees.

sections.heading: Successors: taking over, stepping down, being replaced
sections.body:
- **Taking over.** A willing named successor "is entitled to act as trustee except for good cause or disqualification" and holds all the original trustee's powers and duties (RCW 11.98.039, 11.98.060).
- **Declining.** A named person who has not accepted can decline in writing, delivered to the trustor or, after death or incapacity, to a successor trustee or qualified beneficiary (RCW 11.98.017).
- **Resigning.** A trustee may resign "without judicial proceedings" by a signed writing filed with the trust records (RCW 11.98.029). The trustee is discharged when everyone entitled to notice agrees or 30 days after notice, whichever comes first, unless someone files a court petition before then (RCW 11.98.041).
- **No successor named.** Everyone with an interest can agree in writing on a new trustee, or to add co-trustees (RCW 11.98.039; 11.96A.220).
- **Court.** A beneficiary, the trustor if living, or the trustee can ask the superior court to appoint or change a trustee "for any other reasonable cause" (RCW 11.98.039).
- **Bank mergers.** A named bank's successor in interest is presumed authorized (RCW 11.98.065).

sections.heading: Co-trustees and directed trusts
sections.body:
You can pair an adult child with a trust company. By default, three or more trustees act by majority, a rule that does not help two who disagree. A co-trustee who gets written notice of a proposed action and does not object in writing within 15 days is treated as approving, unless that co-trustee earlier filed a notice opting out of this rule (RCW 11.98.016).

Washington's Uniform Directed Trust Act (chapter 11.98B RCW, which replaced the repealed chapter 11.98A) lets a trust give a "trust director" power over certain decisions, such as investments. The "directed trustee" must then "take reasonable action to comply," but must not comply if doing so would be willful misconduct. A trust can also relieve one co-trustee of liability for another's decisions (RCW 11.98B.050, .080, .110). See [/trustees](/trustees) on co-trustee disagreements about a house.

sections.heading: Questions to weigh
sections.body:
- **Continuity:** Can this person or institution serve in 10 or 20 years? Who is the backup?
- **Family dynamics:** Can one child stay impartial toward siblings, as RCW 11.98.078 requires?
- **Investing:** Can they meet the prudent investor standard? A trustee may hire advisors but must select and monitor them with reasonable care (RCW 11.98.070(27), 11.98.071).
- **Records:** Who will send the notices and yearly statements?

sections.heading: When the trust holds a house
sections.body:
Family and professional trustees face the same rules. Either may sell (RCW 11.98.070), but loyally and prudently. If the house is 25 percent or more of the net fair market value of trust principal, the sale is a "significant nonroutine transaction." Unless a compelling circumstance requires faster action, the trustee must give written notice at least 20 days before signing a binding agreement. Notice goes to the trustor if living and to each adult beneficiary currently receiving income (or having income accumulated) whose address is known. The trustee must also get an independent appraisal or sell on the open market. The trustor or the people entitled to notice can waive these requirements in writing (RCW 11.100.140).

For inherited property, the IRS says basis is generally "the FMV of the property at the date of the individual's death" (Publication 551). Federal law treats property in a trust the decedent could revoke until death, with income payable to the decedent, as acquired from the decedent for this rule (26 U.S.C. § 1014(b)(2)). A date-of-death value therefore matters. See [The House Is in a Living Trust](/washington-probate-guide/house-in-a-trust) and [Probate vs Trust Sale](/guides/probate-vs-trust-sale-washington).

faqs.question: Can a bank be the trustee of my trust in Washington?
faqs.answer: Yes, if it is authorized to do trust business here (RCW 30B.04.030). Ask whether it accepts trusts of your size and type.

faqs.question: Should my oldest child be my successor trustee?
faqs.answer: Whoever serves must act only for the beneficiaries, impartially among them (RCW 11.98.078), invest prudently, and keep everyone informed. Ask whether that child can do this for siblings and has the time. You can also name a backup.

faqs.answer: Yes. With two, the statute's majority rule does not apply, so tie-breaking language matters (RCW 11.98.016). A trust can also make one a directed trustee (chapter 11.98B RCW).

faqs.question: What if the successor trustee doesn't want to serve?
faqs.answer: They can decline in writing before accepting (RCW 11.98.017). If no willing successor is named, everyone with an interest can agree on a new trustee, or a beneficiary can ask the court (RCW 11.98.039).
